title: The Receptor Is the Gene Switch

scenes.visual: Title: The Receptor Is the Gene Switch. Show a hormone, an intracellular receptor and DNA as one connected pathway.

scenes.tts: Nuclear receptors are proteins inside the cell that catch chemical signals and control whether genes are copied into R N A. The receptor itself is a transcription factor. That matters because one receptor can reset many genes at once. New R N A and protein take time to make, so the response builds over hours. But the new proteins remain after the hormone has gone. A steroid hormone crosses the membrane to reach its receptor.

scenes.visual: A steroid hormone crosses the membrane and binds an intracellular receptor. Follow the same receptor to DNA in the nucleus. Show several target genes making RNA and then proteins. A timeline labelled hours advances; remove the hormone while the new proteins remain. Keep the receptor-to-transcription pathway prominent throughout.

scenes.tts: The receptor is one chain with two grips. One region binds the hormone. Another recognizes a specific short stretch of D N A. Most nuclear receptors work in pairs, and their D N A binding site is called a response element. The glucocorticoid receptor pairs with another copy of itself after hormone arrives. The thyroid hormone receptor waits on D N A with a different partner, called R X R. Hormone recognition and D N A recognition are separate jobs in the same protein.

scenes.visual: Keep the receptor design from the opening. Label its hormone-binding domain, hinge and DNA-binding domain. Show a glucocorticoid receptor pair on a response element, then a thyroid hormone receptor paired with RXR on DNA. Use matching colours to connect each domain to its job. Do not imply that every receptor pairs with RXR.

scenes.tts: Hormone binding changes the receptor's shape and which helper proteins it holds. The thyroid hormone receptor releases a co-repressor and brings in a co-activator. These helpers act on chromatin, the packaged form of D N A. Co-activators bring enzymes that add acetyl groups to histones, the proteins D N A wraps around. That loosens the packing and helps R N A polymerase start. Co-repressors bring enzymes that remove those groups. The cell's own mix of helpers also matters.

scenes.visual: Start with the thyroid hormone receptor and RXR already on DNA. Hormone binding replaces a co-repressor with a co-activator. Zoom out to DNA wrapped around histones. Show acetyl badges added, packing loosening and RNA polymerase beginning transcription. In a separate comparison show co-repressors removing acetyl badges. End with different helper pools beside two cells; keep helix 12 out of this overview.

scenes.tts: The family reaches beyond familiar hormones. Some receptors sense the cell's own lipids. P pars bind fatty acids. L X R binds oxidized cholesterol, and F X R binds bile acids. P par gamma drives the making of fat cells. So an intracellular signal can connect to gene control in metabolism, too.

scenes.visual: Expand to a family overview: fatty acids to PPARs, oxidized cholesterol to LXR, and bile acids to FXR. Link each receptor to DNA without inventing downstream effects. Highlight PPAR-gamma with a cell becoming a fat cell. Keep the ligand-to-receptor-to-gene pathway visible.

scenes.tts: That same route meets medicine. Prednisone and dexamethasone act through the glucocorticoid receptor to calm inflammation. Long treatment also raises blood glucose and thins bone. Tissue context matters, too. Tamoxifen blocks estrogen in the breast but imitates it in the uterus and, after menopause, in bone. Its receptor still binds D N A, and the switching surface called A F one can still work. What happens next can depend on the helper proteins each tissue makes. The signal, the receptor and the cell's helpers together shape gene control.

scenes.visual: Show prednisone and dexamethasone acting through the glucocorticoid receptor, with reduced inflammation and a separate long-treatment branch labelled raised blood glucose and thinner bone. Then compare breast, uterus and postmenopausal bone under tamoxifen. Keep receptors on DNA, highlight AF-1 and show different helper pools as a possible explanation of different effects. Finish with signal, receptor on DNA and cellular helpers connected to gene transcription; remove the former helix-12 rule.
End card: The receptor itself controls gene transcription. Repeat the signal-to-receptor-to-DNA image; remove the old groove-availability rule.
